extracted.intended_audience: Prospective NSF GRFP applicants (undergraduates and early graduate students applying for the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for drafting the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship personal statement and research proposal, focusing on narrative coherence, technical clarity, and strategic topic choice. Targeted to applicants preparing submissions (often senior undergraduates or early grad students).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repositories of past successful statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult large repositories of past successful (and unsuccessful) NSF GRFP statements (e.g., Alex Lang's database) to see what works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author used this resource extensively when drafting his application and strongly suggests applicants do the same. This is framed as a defense against survivorship bias — learn from many examples rather than a single opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal statement: comprehensive narrative of intellectual journey
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a reasonably comprehensive narrative of your 'intellectual journey' that unites courses, research, extracurriculars, and other experiences into a coherent story about who you are and what you plan to do next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to tell a story that unites as many of the things you've done as possible; the narrative should serve as connective tissue but be substantive. The story should make clear why your plan going forward 'makes sense.' This is emphasized even if the phrase sounds corny — coherence and connectivity are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make clear why your future plan is sensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Your statement should explicitly show why your proposed next steps are logical and supported by your past experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should be able to see how prior coursework, research, and activities lead to the proposed direction. If you can't convincingly connect disparate experiences, pick a focus that lets you craft a convincing narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an area you can credibly write about
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a general research area for the application that allows you to write a strong personal narrative and an informed proposal (don't try to pivot to an unrelated field in the GRFP application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you've worked in plant biology but want to pivot to human anatomy, the GRFP is probably not the place to make that pivot. No one will hold you to it later, but you should prioritize making the strongest possible application by picking an area aligned with your demonstrated strengths and experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal statement: detailed, specific descriptions of contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The core of the personal statement should contain detailed descriptions of what you specifically did in relevant course, research, and extracurricular experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, specific duties and accomplishments rather than vague statements. Detail helps establish credibility and gives reviewers evidence of skills and potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight awards and publications clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominently call out any awards, publications, or manuscripts in preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends highlighting such achievements in bold to ensure they stand out to reviewers. Emphasize accomplishments that demonstrate research productivity or recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and scope: use the space to be comprehensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect the GRFP personal statement to be lengthy; the author reports his was about 3000 words and advises taking the opportunity to write a reasonably comprehensive narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as probably the longest application you'll write; use the allowed length to include the connective narrative plus detailed descriptions of work. This draft can be repurposed/shortened for other applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal topic: novelty and literature awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a proposal topic you feel comfortable has not already been done in the literature and that you can write confidently about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal should reflect awareness of the existing literature and demonstrate novelty. Avoid proposing work that is already established or that you cannot justify as novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal: write technically for expert evaluators
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your research proposal as the most novel research idea you can describe in technical terms for an audience who will evaluate it on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal should balance novelty with technical clarity so evaluators (who can assess technical merit) can judge the science. Present methodological details and rationale at a level appropriate for expert reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize the person as the investment (people over projects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the application to showcase the applicant as a long-term investment; NSF GRFP invests in people more than projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the proposal matters, emphasize your potential, trajectory, skills, and capacity to complete and extend research. Demonstrate intellectual promise and independence as well as project feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get extensive mentor feedback on the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a research mentor read and comment on your proposal; mentor input is the most effective way to ensure it is cogent and makes a meaningful contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek multiple rounds of feedback from knowledgeable mentors. Mentor review improves technical accuracy, feasibility, and clarity. This is especially emphasized as 'far and away the best way' to improve the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft the best possible (most competitive) proposal before your actual PhD project
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing applications (especially as a senior), write the strongest possible proposal for review even if it is not the exact project you will carry out during your PhD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests crafting a highly competitive proposal first; your subsequent actual research plan can differ. This is a strategic choice to maximize award chances rather than a requirement to commit to that project indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of departmental fit (know your intended department)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a sense of what department you want to end up in, since that can inform how you frame your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes it's helpful to know the target department even if you weren't sure himself; departmental context can help tailor the narrative and proposal to align with likely graduate programs and reviewers' expectations.
